20:    documenting the opacity is correct.

11:  tests interfere with each other, behavior differs between hosts, and the
12:  composition root loses authority over wiring. 12-factor "config in the
13:  environment" applies to the deployable, not to every package.

16:  needed.

18:  - package main and cmd/* composition roots — reading the environment is exactly their job.
19:  - test files using t.Setenv to exercise a composition root.

23:    type Source func(key string) (value string, found bool)
24:    func Load(source Source) (Config, error) { v, ok := source("HELIOS_PORT"); ... }

27:  bad: |

id: go/constructor-purity
class: C1
category: architecture
statement: >-
  A constructor (any exported function whose name is New or starts with New)
  must be pure: it must not directly call time.Now, time.Sleep, timers,
  os.Getenv/LookupEnv/Environ, file I/O (os.Open/ReadFile/WriteFile/Create),

  crypto/rand.Read). All environmental effects enter through injected
  dependencies.

  makes every component substitutable, deterministic to test, and forces the
  composition root to own all wiring. A constructor that reads the clock or
  the environment hides an input and makes behavior untestable without
  patching globals.

id: go/error-wrapping
class: C1
category: idiom
statement: >-
  When propagating an error with added context use fmt.Errorf with the %w verb
  (or errors.Join for aggregation). Never format an error with %v/%s into a new
  error and never concatenate err.Error() — both destroy the error tree, so
  errors.Is/As/AsType stop working for callers.
rationale: >-
  Wrapped errors keep sentinel and typed errors inspectable across package
  boundaries. A %v-formatted error is a dead string: callers can no longer
  branch on the cause, which forces string matching — the canonical Go
  anti-pattern.
applicability: >-
  Any code path that returns an error derived from another error.
exceptions:
  - >-
    Deliberate boundary opacity: when an error must NOT be inspectable (e.g.
    redacting internal detail at an API boundary), formatting with %v and
    documenting the opacity is correct.
  - Log messages (not returned errors) may format errors with %v freely.
example:
  good: |
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("load configuration: %w", err)
    }
  bad: |
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("load configuration: %v", err) // breaks errors.Is/As
    }

  kind: analyzer
  ref: errorwrapping
fix_hint: >-
  Replace the %v/%s verb with %w (fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err)), or use
  errors.Join to aggregate multiple errors.

category: idiom
statement: >-
  An exported interface declares at most 4 methods. Bigger contracts must be
  split into composable single-purpose interfaces (io.Reader/io.Writer style).
rationale: >-
  The bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction (Go proverb). Small
  interfaces are satisfiable by fakes, decorators and adapters; fat interfaces
  force every implementation to stub methods it does not care about and make
  conformance suites combinatorial.
applicability: >-
  Any exported interface type in a library package.
exceptions:

    Interfaces mirroring an external wire contract (a generated client, a
    protocol surface) may exceed the limit; isolate them in the adapter layer.
  - Unexported interfaces are not scored — internal seams may be pragmatic.
example:

    type Reader interface{ Read(p []byte) (int, error) }
    type Closer interface{ Close() error }
    type ReadCloser interface { Reader; Closer }
  bad: |

id: go/return-concrete
class: C1
category: idiom
statement: >-
  Exported functions and constructors return concrete types (or error), not
  project-defined interface types. "Accept interfaces, return structs":
  the consumer decides which interface to view the value through.
rationale: >-
  Returning an interface erases the concrete API surface, blocks method
  additions without breaking callers, defeats inlining, and inverts ownership:
  interfaces belong to consumers, not producers. Returning the struct keeps
  the full API available and lets each caller declare its own narrow seam.
applicability: >-
  Any exported function in a library package whose result is a project-defined
  named interface.
exceptions:
  - error and context.Context are interfaces by design — always allowed.
  - >-
    Standard-library interfaces (io.Reader, slog.Handler, http.Handler, ...)
    are established contracts; returning them is allowed when the function's
    purpose is to produce that contract.
  - >-
    Factories that genuinely select among implementations at runtime may
    return an interface; document why.
example:
  good: |
    func New(cfg Config) (*Cache, error) { ... }   // caller sees the full *Cache API
  bad: |
    type Cacher interface{ Get(string) (string, bool); Put(string, string) }
    func New(cfg Config) (Cacher, error) { ... }   // producer-owned interface
oracle:
  kind: analyzer
  ref: returnconcrete
fix_hint: >-
  Return the concrete *Type; if a caller needs a seam, the caller defines the
  interface next to its own code.

id: go/errors-astype

category: post-cutoff
statement: >-

  errors.AsType[E](err) (Go 1.26), not errors.As(err, &target). AsType is
  type-safe at compile time, needs no pre-declared target variable, and is
  faster.

  errors.As takes any (interface{}) and panics at runtime on a mis-typed
  target; the 1.26 generic form moves that to compile time and reads as a
  single expression. The Go release notes describe it as a "type-safe, faster
  alternative to As". New code on Go >= 1.26 has no reason to use the old form.

    is only known dynamically.

id: go/benchmark-loop
class: C1
category: post-cutoff
statement: >-
  Benchmarks iterate with `for b.Loop()` (Go 1.24), not
  `for i := 0; i < b.N; i++` and not `for range b.N`. b.Loop keeps setup and
  cleanup outside the measured region exactly once and prevents the compiler
  from optimizing the benchmarked call away.
rationale: >-
  The b.N pattern re-runs setup on every benchmark restart, silently measures
  dead code when the compiler proves results unused, and is the single most
  copied stale idiom in Go. b.Loop fixes all three; since Go 1.26 it no longer
  even inhibits inlining.
applicability: >-
  Any *_test.go benchmark on Go >= 1.24.
exceptions:
  - Code that must build on Go < 1.24 keeps b.N.
  - >-
    Benchmarks that intentionally index by iteration (e.g. pre-generated
    inputs[i]) may keep a manual counter alongside b.Loop.
example:
  good: |
    func BenchmarkGet(b *testing.B) {
        c := mustCache(b)
        for b.Loop() { c.Get("k") }
    }
  bad: |
    func BenchmarkGet(b *testing.B) {
        c := mustCache(b)
        for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { c.Get("k") } // stale idiom: setup re-runs, dead-code risk
    }
oracle:
  kind: analyzer
  ref: benchmarkloop
fix_hint: >-
  Replace the b.N loop with `for b.Loop() { ... }` (Go 1.24+).

id: go/waitgroup-go
class: C1
category: post-cutoff
statement: >-
  When spawning one goroutine per task, use sync.WaitGroup.Go(f) (Go 1.25)
  instead of the wg.Add(1) / go func() { defer wg.Done(); ... }() triple.
rationale: >-
  The Add/go/Done triple has two classic failure modes — Add inside the
  goroutine (race with Wait) and a forgotten Done on an early return (deadlock).

applicability: >-

  where the goroutine is created at the call site.
exceptions:

    started elsewhere (worker pools handing tasks to pre-started workers),
    Add/Done remains the correct primitive.

    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for _, input := range inputs {
        wg.Go(func() { process(input) })
    }
    wg.Wait()
  bad: |

    for _, input := range inputs {
